content: 1. Seddon JA et al. (2012) provided practice-based recommendations for managing children with drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). Their work, published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, highlights the challenges and strategies for treating pediatric TB cases resistant to standard drug regimens. 2. Becerra MC et al. (2013) studied the impact of household exposure to multidrug-resistant TB on children. Their findings, published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal, emphasize the importance of early detection and intervention in such high-risk environments. 3. Seddon JA et al. (2012) described the clinical features, treatment approaches, and outcomes of culture-confirmed multidrug-resistant TB in children. This study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, provides critical insights into the complexities of managing pediatric TB cases. 4. Seddon JA et al. (2012) investigated the effect of drug resistance on clinical outcomes in children with tuberculous meningitis. Their research, published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal, underscores the severe implications of drug resistance in this vulnerable population. 5. Ettehad D et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on treatment outcomes for children with multidrug-resistant TB. Published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, this study highlights the variability in treatment success and the need for optimized therapeutic strategies. 6. Schaaf HS, Shean K, and Donald PR (2003) examined diagnostic delays, clinical features, treatment responses, and outcomes in children with culture-confirmed multidrug-resistant TB. Their work, published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood, stresses the importance of timely diagnosis and effective management. 7. Schaaf HS et al. (2002) evaluated young children in contact with adults with multidrug-resistant pulmonary TB over a 30-month follow-up period. Published in Pediatrics, this study highlights the long-term risks and the need for sustained monitoring and care. 8. Swanson DS and Starke JR (1995) reviewed drug-resistant TB in pediatric populations. Their article in Pediatric Clinics of North America provides a comprehensive overview of the challenges and management strategies for this condition. 9. The Guidance for National Tuberculosis Programmes on the Management of Tuberculosis in Children outlines the responsibilities of national TB programs (NTPs) in implementing childhood TB activities. It emphasizes the importance of integrating TB care into family-oriented and community-based approaches, as well as the need for global and national-level actions to improve TB management in children. 10. At the global level, the World Health Organization (WHO) and its partners are tasked with providing training, monitoring tools, and access to diagnostic resources for child TB management. They also assist countries in conducting drug resistance surveys and transitioning to updated drug regimens. 11. At the national level, NTPs are encouraged to develop child-specific TB guidelines, form working groups, evaluate surveillance data, and engage stakeholders to ensure effective implementation and evaluation of TB programs. 12. Accurate recording and reporting of TB cases in children are critical for improving epidemiological surveillance, measuring intervention impacts, and planning pediatric TB services. Children treated for TB should be included in routine NTP recording systems, with data disaggregated by age groups (0–4 years and 5–14 years). 13. Training and supervision of healthcare workers are essential to improve case detection, management, contact screening, and preventive therapy for childhood TB. Training should address common scenarios, such as suspected TB cases, children undergoing treatment, and close contacts of TB cases. 14. Integrated care is vital for managing TB in children, as they often present within maternal and child health or HIV care services rather than specific TB care settings. Collaboration between TB and HIV services is crucial to ensure comprehensive care. 15. Maternal TB during pregnancy increases the risk of TB and HIV transmission to the newborn, as well as adverse outcomes such as preterm delivery and low birth weight. Pregnant women in TB-endemic regions should be screened for TB symptoms, and those diagnosed should begin treatment promptly. 16. Congenital TB, acquired in utero or during delivery, and neonatal TB, acquired postnatally, are challenging to distinguish but require similar management. Symptoms are often nonspecific, and diagnosis relies heavily on maternal history of TB or HIV. 17. Neonates exposed to maternal TB should be screened for disease or latent infection. Separation from the mother is unnecessary unless multidrug-resistant TB is suspected. Breastfeeding can continue, and Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination should be delayed until TB disease is excluded.
